label: gs-academic-paper
topic: Group 1 academic paper: engineering zebrafish, validated lab-in-the-loop with the Delphi system (Lean laws + pre-registered predictions + nanopublications)
summary: Outline written to D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/gs-academic-paper/paper-outline.md from three local sources I opened (BRIEF-2026-11-12.md, tracks/synthesis.json, tracks/research/agents/pp-broad-fish-biologists.json). Key structural finding: none of tracks 1-4 or 6 is currently a zebrafish system (they are MDCK dog-kidney cysts, E. coli soft agar, Cello plasmid gate libraries, autorotating plant fruits), so a zebrafish paper is a re-instantiation of the pipeline in a new organism and must be sold as method-first. Two findings already in hand carry the paper's first figures with no new data: the published vertex-model lumen sweep fails its own reproduction gate (solidity RMSE 0.229 vs 0.124 for a median baseline) and the ported blade-element model's base-angle ratio is already broken by published per-trial data (1.50 measured vs 1.22 predicted). Five claims C1-C5 (lumen geometry, reproduction-gate failure, reporter threshold/steepness separability, pattern spacing, fin/body constraint) each get a minimal fish experiment with line, readout, n, dpf window and cost class, plus an 8-point sign-off list for a fish biologist. The honesty hazard is the formal layer: 14 of 59 pinned laws have no Lean theorem at all, including exactly the gene-regulatory-dynamics and fin-length-ratio laws two claims lean on. Venue scope statements were NOT opened in the time available, so venues are candidates only.

key_claims: No zebrafish data exists yet in any track, so the paper must lead with the method and the two existing negative results, not with a fish result.
The published lumen vertex-model fails its own reproduction gate (0.229 vs 0.124), which is a figure the group already owns.
14 of 59 pinned laws have no Lean theorem, including the two the molecular and organism claims depend on, so a law-audit table must be in the main text.
The three weakest points a reviewer will attack: the fish framing is a graft; 'machine-checked law' overclaims; the negative results may be our own re-implementation errors.
lay_summary: Our group wants to write a science paper about changing a tiny see-through fish on purpose, and then checking the changes against rules about living things that a computer has proved are logically correct.
When we looked at the work we already have, none of it is actually about fish yet: it is about dog kidney cells in a dish, bacteria in jelly, bits of DNA circuitry, and spinning plant seeds.
So the paper should really be about our checking machine, with the fish as its first living test, and we say that out loud instead of pretending we already have fish results.
We do already have two useful surprises: when we rebuilt two published computer models, neither one matched the published measurements, and those misses can be the paper's first pictures.

Before touching a single fish, a real fish scientist has to agree the fish lines, ages, measurements and animal rules make sense, and we also have to admit that many of our 'proved' rules are not actually proved yet.

glossary.zebrafish: A small see-through freshwater fish used to study how bodies develop.
glossary.dpf: Days post-fertilisation: how many days old a fish embryo or larva is.
glossary.lumen: The hollow space inside a tube in the body, like a gut or a duct.
glossary.solidity: A shape number: how much of a shape's outline is filled in rather than dented.
glossary.RMSE: Root-mean-square error: the average size of a model's mistakes, in the units of the thing measured.
glossary.vertex model: A computer model that treats cells as polygons meeting at corners and lets them pull on each other.
glossary.MDCK cysts: Hollow balls of dog kidney cells grown in gel, used as a stand-in for a tube in the body.
glossary.Lean: A computer language in which a mathematical statement can be proved, so the proof is machine-checked.
glossary.law set: The frozen, numbered list of biology statements this project treats as its laws.
glossary.pinned law: A law included in a particular numbered law set; it may or may not have an actual proof attached.
glossary.nanopublication: A tiny machine-readable published claim with its evidence and who said it.
glossary.pre-registered prediction: A prediction written down and frozen before the data is looked at, so it cannot be adjusted afterwards.
glossary.reproduction gate: A pass/fail test that a published model must survive on the original data before anyone builds on it.
glossary.Hill coefficient: A number describing how steeply a biological response switches on as its input rises.
glossary.dose-response: The curve relating how much of a signal you give to how much response you get.
glossary.ribosome binding site: The short DNA/RNA stretch that sets how often a gene's message gets translated into protein.
glossary.reporter: A gene added so that cells glow or change colour when something happens, making it visible.
glossary.transgenic line: A strain of animals carrying an added piece of DNA, bred so all of them have it.
glossary.Gal4/UAS: A two-part genetic switch used to turn an added gene on only in chosen cells.
glossary.apical surface: The face of a cell that lines the inside of a tube.
glossary.Laplace pressure: The relation between pressure inside a bubble or tube, its tension, and its curvature.
glossary.diffusion-driven instability: A mechanism where two spreading chemicals at different speeds spontaneously create stripes or spots (also called Turing patterning).
glossary.Fisher-KPP: A classic equation for how a growing population spreads as a travelling front.
glossary.blade-element model: A way of predicting the forces on a wing or fin by adding up thin slices of it.
glossary.clutch: One batch of eggs from one mating; fish from the same clutch are not independent samples.
glossary.confocal: A microscope that takes sharp slices through a thick sample to build a 3D image.
glossary.Crossref DOI: A permanent identifier for a published paper, checkable against a public registry.
glossary.in silico: Done entirely on a computer, with no lab work.
glossary.validity domain: The range of conditions in which a law has actually been shown to hold.

recommendations: Lead the paper with the method and the two existing reproduction failures; do not claim a fish result in the title or abstract until C1's wild-type pilot exists.
Put the law-set audit (which of 59 pinned laws are machine-checked, which are placeholders) in the main text as a figure, before a reviewer finds it.
Run C2 (rerun the published lumen sweep end to end with fixed seeds) this week: no lab, no fish, and it decides whether figure 2 stands.
Close the Lean gaps for gene-regulatory-dynamics and fin-length-ratio, or restate C3 and C5 as unproved registry claims.
Get a fish biologist's written sign-off on tube choice, stage window, line identity, drug doses, exclusion criteria, animal-protocol scope and clutch-as-replicate before freezing any prediction.
Gate the expensive transgenesis arm (C3) on C1 reproducing in wild type.

Open each candidate venue's scope page and paste the verbatim scope sentence into the outline before choosing a target; post to bioRxiv first with freeze timestamps and nanopublication IDs in the abstract.
Publish the diff between our re-implementation and the original authors' code for both negative results, and ask the original authors for seeds and loading assumptions.
